title: Learned tract maps link postoperative network changes with language changes
summary: In a small retrospective subgroup of 21 children undergoing epilepsy surgery, changes in model-defined white-matter networks were associated with changes in language scores. Combined language-network efficiency changes correlated with core language-score changes at R=.674. Both pre- and postoperative scans were used; this was not a preoperative prediction of future outcomes.

source_review.scope: Original full-text clinical cohort and nonprocedural computational/statistical Methods and Results; model output distinguished from association and treatment effects.

evidence.tested: An 85-child preoperative tractography cohort supplied 47 training, 20 test and 18 later temporal-validation cases. Separate clinical analyses included 45 children with paired scans and 21 with paired scans/language assessments. In the 21-child language analysis, learned tract maps defined connectivity networks, and ordinary Pearson analysis related efficiency changes to core language-score changes (R=.674, P<.001). CCA additionally fitted multivariate associations on these data.
evidence.unknown: The 21-child association is an exploratory within-study analysis, with multiple network/language comparisons and no stated independent CCA holdout. It uses postoperative imaging and cannot predict an unknown postoperative result from preoperative data alone. Clinical management was blinded to the analysis and was not altered. Cohort/scanner specificity, varying follow-up and incomplete outcome data limit generalization; surgical benefit, optimal margins and causal language effects were not established.
evidence.ai_role: A learned tract classifier identified language-pathway groups; conventional network measures and correlation analysis then related imaging changes to measured language changes.
